name: Sakhir
history: Built in the desert south of Manama, Sakhir opened in 2004 and gave the Middle East its first Grand Prix. It has since become a regular season-opener and pre-season test venue.
facts: The race has run at night under floodlights since 2014.
In 2020 the outer loop, a lap of just 3.543 km, hosted the one-off Sakhir Grand Prix.

name: Jeddah
history: Laid out along the Red Sea waterfront and first raced in 2021, Jeddah was built in under a year. It is a street circuit with the flow of a permanent track.
facts: It is the fastest street circuit on the calendar, with average speeds above 250 km/h.
Its 27 corners are the most of any current layout.

name: Melbourne
history: Albert Park took over the Australian Grand Prix from Adelaide in 1996. The track runs on public park roads around a lake, closed off each year for race week.
facts: The circuit was reprofiled in 2022 to make it faster and better for overtaking.
For the rest of the year you can drive most of the lap at the city speed limit.

name: Suzuka
history: Honda built Suzuka in 1962 as a test track, and it first hosted the Japanese Grand Prix in 1987. Many world titles have been settled here.
facts: It is the only figure-eight layout on the calendar, crossing itself on a bridge.
130R is one of the fastest corners in racing, taken almost flat out.

name: Shanghai
history: Opened in 2004 on reclaimed marshland, Shanghai brought Formula 1 to mainland China. The layout traces the character 上, the first in the city's name.
facts: Turns 1 and 2 form a tightening spiral of almost 270 degrees.
The back straight is about 1.2 km long, one of the longest of the year.

name: Miami
history: Built around Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, the circuit joined the calendar in 2022. It is a temporary track made for the race each spring.
facts: The first year's paddock featured a fake marina, with painted water and no sea.
The lap has 19 corners and three long straights.

name: Montréal
history: Laid out on the man-made Île Notre-Dame in 1978, the track was later named after Canadian driver Gilles Villeneuve. It mixes long straights with tight chicanes.
facts: The final chicane's outer wall is nicknamed the Wall of Champions after several title holders hit it in 1999.
The 2011 race lasted over four hours with its rain delay, the longest in the sport's history.

name: Monaco
history: First run in 1929 and part of the championship since 1950, Monaco runs through the streets of Monte Carlo. Qualifying matters more here than almost anywhere.
facts: It is the only race well short of the usual 305 km distance.
The Fairmont hairpin is the slowest corner in Formula 1, taken at about 50 km/h.

name: Portimão
history: Opened in 2008 in the hills of the Algarve, Portimão first hosted Formula 1 in 2020 and 2021. It returns to the calendar from 2027.
facts: Its sharp crests and drops earn it the nickname of the rollercoaster.
Lewis Hamilton took his record 92nd win here in 2020.

name: Silverstone
history: Silverstone began as a wartime RAF airfield and hosted the first ever World Championship race on 13 May 1950. The runways still shape parts of the lap.
facts: The Maggotts, Becketts and Chapel sequence is one of the great high-speed sections in racing.
Most Formula 1 teams have their factories within an hour's drive.

name: Spielberg
history: The Österreichring opened here in 1969, was shortened into the A1-Ring in 1997, and returned as the Red Bull Ring in 2014. It sits on a hillside in the Styrian mountains.
facts: Lap times are among the shortest of the year, a little over a minute.
The lap climbs about 65 m from the start to the top of the hill.

name: Spa-Francorchamps
history: Spa first used public roads in the Ardennes forest in 1921, on a lap of almost 15 km. The modern track keeps much of the old character and is the longest on the calendar.
facts: Eau Rouge and Raidillon climb steeply uphill and are taken nearly flat out.
It can rain on one part of the track while another stays dry.

name: Hungaroring
history: The Hungaroring hosted the first Formula 1 race behind the Iron Curtain in 1986. It sits in a valley outside Budapest, so spectators can see much of the lap.
facts: Its tight, twisting lap is often called Monaco without the walls.
It has hosted a Grand Prix every year since 1986.

name: Monza
history: Built in a royal park in 1922, Monza is called the Temple of Speed. Only one season since 1950 has not had an Italian Grand Prix here.
facts: The fastest average lap in Formula 1 history was set here, over 264 km/h.
The old banked oval still stands, crumbling, in the trees beside the track.

name: Madrid
history: Madring is a new semi-street circuit around the IFEMA exhibition centre, first raced in 2026. It brought the Spanish Grand Prix to the capital.
facts: La Monumental is a steeply banked corner built for the track.
The lap mixes public roads with sections built just for racing.

name: Baku
history: Baku first held a race in 2016, as the European Grand Prix, before taking its own name in 2017. The lap runs past the old walled city and along the Caspian seafront.
facts: The castle section narrows to about 7.6 m between the walls.
A run of about 2.2 km flat out makes it one of the fastest tracks of the year.

name: Istanbul Park
history: Opened in 2005 on the Asian side of Istanbul, the track ran until 2011 and returned in 2020 and 2021. It runs anticlockwise over rolling ground.
facts: Turn 8 is a long four-apex left-hander that loads drivers' necks for several seconds.
Lewis Hamilton sealed his seventh world title here in 2020.

name: Singapore
history: In 2008 Marina Bay held Formula 1's first night race, lit by floodlights through the city. It is one of the longest and most demanding races of the year.
facts: Drivers can lose around 3 kg of fluid in the heat and humidity.
The race often runs close to the two-hour limit.

name: Austin
history: Circuit of the Americas opened in 2012 as the first track in the United States built for Formula 1. It borrows ideas from famous corners elsewhere.
facts: Turn 1 sits at the top of a steep climb of about 40 m.
The opening esses take after Silverstone's Maggotts and Becketts.

name: Mexico City
history: The track is named after racing brothers Ricardo and Pedro Rodríguez and first held a championship race in 1963. It sits in a city park at about 2,240 m.
facts: The thin air cuts downforce and cooling, so cars run high wing settings.
The final sector runs through a baseball stadium full of fans.

name: Interlagos
history: Interlagos, between two lakes in São Paulo, has hosted the Brazilian Grand Prix on and off since 1973. It is a short, anticlockwise lap with big elevation changes.
facts: The opening downhill left-right is called the S do Senna, after Ayrton Senna.
Many title deciders have been held here, often in sudden rain.

name: Las Vegas
history: Las Vegas returned to Formula 1 in 2023 with a Saturday-night race down the Strip. The city had hosted two races in a Caesars Palace car park in 1981 and 1982.
facts: The main straight runs about 1.9 km past the casinos.
Night temperatures in November can fall below 10 °C, making tyres hard to warm.

name: Lusail
history: Lusail was built in 2004 for motorcycle racing and first hosted Formula 1 in 2021. The race runs at night under floodlights.
facts: The lap is mostly fast, flowing corners with only one long straight.
It was the first track in the world floodlit for night motorcycle racing.

name: Yas Marina
history: Yas Marina opened in 2009 with a race that begins at sunset and ends under lights. It usually closes the season.
facts: A hotel straddles the track, and cars pass underneath it.
The pit exit runs through a tunnel under the circuit.

name: Nürburgring
history: The modern Grand Prix circuit opened in 1984 beside the old track in the Eifel hills. It hosted German, European, Luxembourg and Eifel Grands Prix until 2020.
facts: The original Nordschleife lap is about 20.8 km, and Jackie Stewart called it the Green Hell.
Formula 1 left the Nordschleife after Niki Lauda's fiery crash there in 1976.

name: Le Mans
history: Le Mans has hosted its 24-hour race since 1923, much of it on public roads closed for the week. It is the oldest active endurance race in the world.
facts: The record distance is 397 laps, over 5,400 km, set in 2010.
Formula 1 raced here once, in 1967, on the short Bugatti Circuit.

name: Imola
history: Imola, named after Enzo Ferrari and his son Dino, hosted the San Marino Grand Prix from 1981 to 2006. The 1994 weekend, when Roland Ratzenberger and Ayrton Senna were killed, changed safety in the sport.
facts: It is one of the few anticlockwise tracks in Formula 1.
The Tamburello bend, once flat out, became a chicane after 1994.

name: Zandvoort
history: Zandvoort was built in the coastal dunes in 1948, partly on wartime roads. Formula 1 came back in 2021 after a 36-year gap.
facts: The final banked corner leans up to 18 degrees.
Sand blows onto the track from the dunes, so grip changes all weekend.

name: Indianapolis
history: Indianapolis opened in 1909, and the Indy 500 counted toward the World Championship from 1950 to 1960.
facts: The track was paved with about 3.2 million bricks in 1909, hence the Brickyard.
Only six cars started the 2005 race after a tyre dispute.
Formula 1 used a road course inside the oval from 2000 to 2007.

name: Hockenheim
history: Hockenheim opened in 1932 and hosted the German Grand Prix often from 1970 to 2019. Until 2001 its lap ran deep into the forest on long straights.
facts: The old forest layout was about 6.8 km long.
The Motodrom stadium section seats tens of thousands around the final corners.
